catalog_quote: Stress, in the sense of the presence within the word of a syllable nucleus bearing increased amplitude, pitch excursion or length, is not contrastive in Wutung. That is, there are no lexical items which contrast solely on the basis of the placement of such stress. However, there is phonetic stress, with each word able to bear only a single primary stress. Typically the primary stress appears in penultimate position. This location is mainly a feature of tri-syllabic words and also found on disyllabic words, although in rapid speech these latter may be heard as having even stress. Words of greater than two syllables always exhibit prominence on one of them, however this is neither regular nor predictable. While individual speakers tend to have preferred patterns for some words this varies quite freely, both between speakers and within idiolects. ... Of course, it is possible that there is some sort of regularity to stress assignment, but if so it is very complex and involves an interaction between prosody (both lexical tone and intonation) and pragmatic factors. Chapter 5 presents an analysis of tone which incorporates a tone-attracting accent which is always present on the second syllable of polysyllabic words. This accent does not appear to manifest in any other way; stress is not audibly present on the second syllable any more than on any other syllable. Nor has any acoustic evidence for this accent been found, either in terms of length or amplitude.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Wutung is a word-tone language (four melodies H, L, HL, LHL mapped onto the word, with an optional pitch-attracting accent point on the first or second syllable). Stress is not contrastive and not predictable: each word carries one phonetic primary stress, most often on the penultimate syllable in di- and trisyllables, but its position varies freely between speakers and within a speaker (e.g. hlapä ~ hla pä 'night'), and the author codes the language as 'no fixed stress' / 'not predictable' / 'no rhythmic stress' for WALS-14/15/17 (App. A.2, pp. 354-355). The tonal accent point is not realised as stress (no audible prominence, no length or amplitude correlate found).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the source says each word bears 'only a single primary stress' and, in App. A.2, that there is 'no rhythmic stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Placement varies freely between and within speakers without contrast; disyllables in rapid speech may sound evenly stressed; stress placement affects the realisation of certain segment strings, e.g. /w/ in huwur 'stomach' [hu'we] ~ [hu:e] (§3.2.3, p. 52). The author adds that any regularity, if it exists, 'is very complex and involves an interaction between prosody (both lexical tone and intonation) and pragmatic factors' (p. 91).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word delimited by hiatus-avoidance glottal/glide insertion, §3.5); citation-form and text data. Intonation is explicitly not treated systematically (§5.1, p. 153). Minor internal tension: §3.6 p. 91 says the tone-attracting accent 'is always present on the second syllable of polysyllabic words', whereas §5.5.1.2 p. 165 says words bear no accent, or an accent on the first or second syllable; either way it is a tonal-association device, not stress. Cf. Marmion's own footnote 28 (p. 91) comparing the free-stress situation to Mpur (Odé 2002) and Awa Pit (Curnow 1997).
new_statements.identity_note: Marmion 2010 describes the Wutung-village lect (about 580-600 speakers, Sandaun Province, PNG). The closely related, mutually intelligible Musu and Nyao village lects (thesis §1, Fig. 1.7-1.8; Table 3.5 'Wutung vs Musu lects') are treated as dialects of the same language; the thesis data are from Wutung village proper. Matches Glottolog wutu1244 (ISO wut). Not to be confused with Skou (skou1243) across the border or Vanimo/Dusur (vani1248).

sources.note: §3.6 'Stress' pp. 90-91: stress is not contrastive; there is phonetic stress, one primary stress per word, 'typically' penultimate (mainly in trisyllables, also disyllables), but placement is 'neither regular nor predictable', varies freely between and within speakers (hlapä ~ hla pä 'night'); a tone-attracting accent point (ch. 5, §5.5.1.2 pp. 165-166, on 1st or 2nd syllable, or absent) has no audible or acoustic stress correlate. App. A.2 pp. 354-355: author codes WALS-14 'no fixed stress', WALS-15 'not predictable', WALS-17 'no rhythmic stress'. Four word-tone melodies H, L, HL, LHL.
